overview: This is the modern Republic of Armenia, whose independence referendum took place on 21 September 1991, before this map record begins in 1994. It is distinct from Soviet Armenia and the First Republic of 1918 to 1920. The imported “Sasanian E” alias is erroneous. Coarse outlines from 1994, 2000 and 2010 cannot establish present legal borders or resolve the changing history of the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict.

periods.title: Independence before this map interval
periods.summary: The independence referendum and state-building process preceded the imported 1994 start.

periods.title: Building the republic
periods.summary: The 1995 constitution and its 2005 amendments structured the new state.

periods.title: A revised constitutional framework
periods.summary: The constitutional text adopted in December 2015 reworked the institutions of government.

periods.title: Displacement, care and rebuilding
periods.summary: The September 2023 refugee influx created large needs for housing, schooling and care. This is a continuing chapter, not a predicted end of the republic.

items.text: Armenia entered the United Nations on 2 March 1992. Membership offers a clear milestone in the republic’s international history, separate from the date when a particular atlas happens to begin drawing its outline.

The 2015 constitutional text gives the National Assembly a role in choosing the prime minister, who directs government policy and coordinates ministers. These written rules describe the organization of public power; the text itself is not evidence that every constitutional promise is always fulfilled.

Written Armenian: իշխանությունը պատկանում է ժողովրդին ,  išxanutʿyunə patkanum ē žołovrdin, “power belongs to the people.” These words come from Article 2 of the official constitutional text adopted on 6 December 2015. The excerpt preserves the Armenian spelling; the official English version provides the translation.

UNESCO’s 2014 description of lavash shows bread-making as coordinated work. Bakers stretch a thin sheet of flour-and-water dough over an oval cushion and slap it onto a clay oven’s inner wall. It bakes in roughly thirty seconds to one minute: this bread requires close attention!

The same account describes women baking together, younger girls helping and learning, and men making cushions or building ovens. These are documented patterns of sharing skills, not rules for every household. A loaf depends on tools, building knowledge and teamwork as well as a baker.

Lavash can wrap cheese, greens or meat. In the wedding practice described by UNESCO, it is also placed on newlyweds’ shoulders with wishes for fertility and prosperity. Bread can be both food for a meal and part of how a family marks a new beginning.

TUMO describes a free educational program where teenagers combine self-directed activities, workshops and project laboratories. Its founders, Sam and Sylva Simonian, grew up in Beirut and later moved to the United States. Their educational project is one concrete link between Armenia and its wider diaspora.

Armenian letters can become art as well as sentences. UNESCO’s 2019 record describes ornamental letters shaped like birds, animals, knots and imaginary creatures, used by craftspeople including embroiderers, sculptors and jewelers. Learning to recognize a letter might occasionally involve spotting its beak!

Modern archaeological research brought an ancient shoe back into view. In 2008, a team at Areni-1 cave found a complete leather shoe in a prehistoric pit. Published analysis dated its leather to approximately 3627 to 3377 BCE. This was a modern discovery of ancient life, not an invention by the modern republic.

The Areni shoe was made from one piece of leather and had taken the shape of a right foot. Grass packed inside may have helped it keep its shape in storage. The researchers could not securely identify the wearer’s sex: even a well-preserved shoe does not tell its owner’s whole story.

sections.title: School toilets and healthcare that travels

items.text: A UNICEF assessment begun in 2023 examined 350 schools and preschools in Lori, Syunik, Gegharkunik and Yerevan. Among assessed schools, 86 percent lacked sanitation accessible to students with disabilities. This is a finding about the surveyed institutions, not a census of every school in Armenia.

In January 2025, accessible mobile restroom units arrived at schools in Hovk and Hermon. Hovk’s earlier toilet had a rocky access path, and its washing pipe was attached to a tree. The new model addressed privacy, handwashing and access together rather than simply adding another door.

The mobile toilet design solves an unusual problem: a school may need decent bathrooms now even when its building will later be replaced. UNICEF explains that the unit can move to another site after a rebuilt school gains indoor facilities. Even a bathroom can have a second assignment.

WHO’s March 2024 account describes mobile mental-health teams visiting communities affected by the refugee influx. A social worker from Karabakh worked with a psychiatrist and psychologists. Care involved helping people with grief, stress and longer-term conditions, bringing services closer to families rather than expecting everyone to travel.

Between November 2023 and February 2024, outreach teams also brought consultations and flu vaccination to older people and people with chronic conditions in shelters and care facilities. WHO describes a 75-year-old woman receiving vaccination alongside her family in a former kindergarten used as a shelter.

A joint statement by Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia declared a ceasefire effective on 10 November 2020 in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict zone. Its provisions addressed military positions, peacekeeping and movement. This is a dated agreement; its terms should not be mistaken for a description of today’s situation.

In September 2023, more than 100,000 refugees arrived in Armenia from Karabakh within one week, according to UNHCR. Receiving communities had to find housing, classroom places and services at extraordinary speed. Refugee experience is part of the republic’s recent history, not an interchangeable label for all its residents.

On 11 August 2025, Armenia’s foreign ministry published the initialed Armenia-Azerbaijan peace agreement by mutual agreement of the parties. Publication and initialing are specific diplomatic steps. This dated record alone does not establish that every provision had been ratified or put into effect.

ending.text: The Republic of Armenia continues as a state and United Nations member. Its modern history includes constitutional change, cultural work, scientific research and the demands of caring for displaced families. Neither a map snapshot ending in 2020 nor this card’s historical phases mark the country’s disappearance.
